extracted.intended_audience: general readers and citizens interested in political theory and reform (late-18th-century public)
extracted.subtask_description: A political pamphlet arguing against hereditary monarchy and mixed government and defending representative/republican government, fiscal prudence, and popular accountability. It sets out normative standards for what makes a legitimate, effective, and just government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary succession is illegitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights of men in society are neither devisable or transferable, nor annihilable, but are descendable only; therefore hereditary succession attempted as a will of a prior generation is an absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine argues that a former generation cannot, by its will or testament, take from the commencing generation their rights and give them to a third person ("A cannot make a will to take from B the property of B, and give it to C"). Hereditary claims based on bequests of rights are legally and morally invalid; rights do not have legal descent in the sense of being alienable by will.

rubrics_metrics.name: A generation cannot bind successors by bequest
rubrics_metrics.description: The generation that first selects a person to govern acts as a free agent for itself and has no right to change itself into a testator to bequeath government to succeeding generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first generation that establishes a government cannot convert the collective act of selection into a testamentary transfer that binds future generations; attempting to do so assumes a character for which it has neither right nor title and undermines the free agency of succeeding generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government must be justified by the services it performs
rubrics_metrics.description: If monarchy is a necessary thing, its necessity must be shown by the services it performs; if unnecessary or merely expensive, it is unjustified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine demands practical justification: 'If it is necessary, in what does that necessity consist, what service does it perform, what is its business, and what are its merits?' Mere symbols (crowns, titles) do not establish necessity. Evaluate institutions by concrete functions and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government should be based on reason not ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: Republican government rests on reason, while hereditary succession rests on ignorance; the better form is that which accords with human reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine states the two forms of government erect themselves on two opposite bases—Reason and Ignorance—and asserts that a well-constituted republic 'requires no belief from man beyond what his reason can give.' Use intelligible principles rather than superstition or imposed belief to justify governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talents and abilities cannot be hereditary
rubrics_metrics.description: Because talents and abilities cannot have hereditary descent, hereditary succession is incompatible with the requirements of government which require talents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective government 'requires talents and abilities'—qualities not transmissible by birth. Therefore hereditary government rests on an impossible premise and must rely on ignorance to be maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign sovereigns are unsuitable rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Importing a foreign sovereign is inadvisable because a foreigner cannot understand the country's laws, manners, or language and will have conflicting interests in their original dominions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine asks rhetorically how a foreigner can understand domestic affairs and points out the natural conflict of interests (e.g., Hanoverian succession). If a nation contemplates a foreign ruler, conditions (such as abandoning foreign estates) should at least be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy is often an expensive sinecure benefiting courtiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Monarchy frequently functions as a costly burden on the nation, providing salaries and sinecures for placemen, pensioners, and court favourites while contributing little to internal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine notes England's high taxes and the paradox that most internal government is carried out by the people via magistrates and juries, while monarchy's costs persist. Evaluate monarchy against its fiscal burden and the actual services delivered to ordinary people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government tends to operate by corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed governments (combining monarchy, aristocracy, representation) necessarily rely on corruption to 'cement' discordant parts and keep them functioning together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because mixed systems give exercise to both reason and hereditary privilege, the hereditary parts require buying-off of reason ('it becomes necessary to buy the reason up'). Expect patronage, places, pensions, and compromises as the moving power of such systems; this undermines integrity and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real constitutions must be fixed and referable
rubrics_metrics.description: A true constitution should be referable and resolvable by producing that constitution; mere canting use of the word 'Constitution' in Parliament indicates absence of a real constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine criticises English parliamentary use of 'Constitution' as inconsistent—if there were a constitution debates would terminate by referring to it. Criterion: constitutional claims must be grounded in an authoritative, accessible document or settled reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative bodies are organs of the nation, not the nation itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions like the House of Commons are organs through which the Nation acts and therefore cannot possess inherent, indefeasible rights independent of the Nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine warns against absorbing the rights of the Nation into an organ (e.g., Parliament or Commons). When organs claim supremacy, they supplant national sovereignty; evaluate whether bodies act as representatives or as self-constituted sovereigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: A government relying on an unaccountable part 'that can do no wrong' lacks responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When any part of government (e.g., the King) is placed beyond culpability (maxim 'a King can do no wrong'), responsibility is removed and governance becomes irresponsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine explains how immunities shift blame to ministers who then shelter under parliamentary majorities. Criterion: accountability must attach to actors; immunities that prevent redress or punishment indicate defective constitutional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed governments devolve into government by committee with blurred roles
rubrics_metrics.description: In mixed governments the advisers, actors, approvers, justifiers, and responsible/unresponsible persons become the same, producing a committee-like machine lacking separation of roles and responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect overlapping offices and conflicts of interest; this structural conflation corrodes checks and balances. Evaluate institutional design for clear role separation to preserve responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding (public debt) systems that create paper currency are fragile
rubrics_metrics.description: The funding system creates sums on paper and depends on a tax to keep the 'imaginary capital' alive; if the public disposition to pay taxes ends, that 'credit' collapses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine asserts the funding system is neither real money nor true credit—it's sustained by people's willingness to be taxed. Assess public finance by specie (coin) foundations and sustainability of tax consent rather than by nominal funded debt alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nation and government solvency are distinct; creditors should look to the nation
rubrics_metrics.description: A government may be insolvent while the nation remains rich; in revolutions creditors attached to the government may be paid by the nation which becomes the real pay-master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine uses the French example: although the old government was insolvent, the nation retained means and the National Assembly treated creditors as creditors of the nation, not merely of the fallen government. When assessing credit risk, evaluate the permanence of national resources, not just regime stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal reform should include cutting expenses and seizing/selling corrupt/privileged property
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing government expenses and selling monastic and ecclesiastical landed estates can raise funds and reduce interest obligations, improving national finances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine cites the French National Assembly's sale of church lands and expense reductions as concrete measures that reduced annual interest on the debt by millions. Practical fiscal remedies: expense cuts and redirecting concentrated privileged wealth toward public service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularity is often driven by resentment, not merit; beware temper-based national decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion shifts can be driven by resentment (e.g., coalition hatreds) rather than considered principle; nations may act on temper rather than fixed principles, producing unstable policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine distinguishes two species of popularity—'excited by merit' and 'by resentment'—and warns that actions taken from sudden public temper can lead to inconsistent continuance of rash measures. Evaluate political choices for principled grounding rather than transient passions.
